analysis.one_liner: Bans open-market stock buybacks and gives workers seats on corporate boards.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when that Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The Reward Work Act would do two things. First, it would outlaw the common corporate practice of a company buying back its own shares on the stock market — a practice that has funneled hundreds of billions of dollars a year back to shareholders and that critics say would otherwise go to higher wages or investment. Second, it would require every public company to let its employees elect one-third of the board of directors, giving workers a direct vote in corporate decisions for the first time. It was introduced by Sen. Tammy Baldwin with three original cosponsors and never moved past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees of public companies, who would gain the right to elect one-third of their company's board and a voice in decisions about pay, layoffs, and buybacks. Workers and communities more broadly could benefit if money currently spent repurchasing stock were redirected toward wages, hiring, or productive investment. Shareholders who believe buybacks inflate stock prices at the expense of long-term company health would also gain.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any public company from purchasing its own shares on a national securities exchange, and it voids the existing SEC safe-harbor rule (Rule 10b-18) that shields companies from market-manipulation liability when they run buyback programs.

The bill amends securities registration law so that no company may list on a national exchange unless at least one-third of its board of directors is chosen by employees in a one-employee-one-vote election, with the SEC and National Labor Relations Board writing rules to make those elections fair and to complete the transition within two years.
Tender offers — a company offering to buy back shares directly from holders — would remain legal, so the ban targets the day-to-day open-market repurchases that dominate modern buyback activity.

analysis.who_pays: Public companies and their executives, whose stock-based compensation is closely tied to share prices that buybacks push up, and shareholders who receive buyback proceeds. Investment banks and trading firms that earn fees designing and executing buyback programs would lose that business. Companies would also have to share board control with worker-elected directors.
analysis.who_pays_short: Public companies, executives, and large shareholders

drawbacks.text: Buybacks are not simply a cash drain: they are a flexible way to return profits to shareholders, including the pension funds and retirement accounts of ordinary workers, and economists genuinely dispute whether restricting them would meaningfully raise investment or wages.
The ban leaves tender offers untouched, so buybacks could shift to that channel, which critics note is less transparent than open-market repurchases and could blunt the bill's purpose.

Requiring one-third of every board to be elected by employees is a sweeping change to corporate governance that opponents argue could reduce board expertise and make companies less attractive to investors, with compliance costs for thousands of listed firms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give workers real power inside the companies that employ them and strike at a practice that critics link to stagnant wages and stock-price-driven executive pay. The cost is real but debatable: shareholders — including ordinary people's retirement funds — would receive less cash from buybacks, and companies would run under a new governance model whose effects are uncertain. The design has a gap, since buybacks could migrate to tender offers. On balance, it is a substantial shift of corporate power toward workers, with honest questions about how the buyback ban would behave in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it expired with the Congress without ever reaching the Senate floor.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Baldwin introduced the Reward Work Act in the Senate on March 27, 2019, joined by original cosponsors Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Kirsten Gillibrand, and Bernie Sanders.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs that same day.
No further action appears in the record: the committee held no markup, reported nothing, and the full Senate never considered the bill before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public companies and their executives are better off: they kept the right to repurchase their own shares on the open market — a practice running to hundreds of billions of dollars a year — and kept boards with no employee representation. Workers gained nothing from this bill's death.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred; all four Senate sponsors were Democrats and an independent, and the Republican-led committee declined to take the bill up, so the fight never took a partisan shape on the record.

industries.note: The bill would end open-market buybacks, which executives with stock-based pay rely on to lift share prices, and would give employees one-third of board seats. Their loss is workers' direct gain in corporate control.

Buybacks are a major source of returns to shareholders, including retirement funds held by ordinary people, and those would end; some shareholders, however, argue buybacks starve companies of long-term investment.
These firms design and execute buyback programs for fees; the ban would remove that business. Their loss imposes no cost on ordinary people.
